questions.title: Bladder exstrophy, epispadias and prune-belly syndrome
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Bladder exstrophy, epispadias and prune-belly syndrome

Classical exstrophy has an exposed bladder plate, epispadias, pubic diastasis, abnormal pelvic floor and genital configuration. Variants include covered/duplicate or superior vesical fissure forms and cloacal exstrophy. Initial care protects the bladder plate with nonadherent moist material, avoids abrasive dressings and assesses kidneys, genitalia, pelvis and associated bowel/spinal disease. Document plate size/quality and upper-tract status.

Reconstruction aims at low-pressure storage, safe renal drainage, functional genitalia and eventual continence. Options include staged closure followed by epispadias and bladder-neck reconstruction, or complete primary repair in experienced centres. Pelvic osteotomy can reduce closure tension in selected age/anatomy. Delayed presenters require assessment of plate viability, capacity and prior operations; augmentation or diversion may be appropriate when native reconstruction cannot give safe storage. Diversion includes catheterizable continent reconstruction and selected incontinent conduits; each carries long-term renal/metabolic consequences.

Mitchell complete penile disassembly mobilises the urethral plate from the corporal bodies, permits correction of epispadias and corporal rotation, and repositions the plate ventrally. Protect neurovascular structures; risks include ischaemia, glans/urethral injury and sexual/continence consequences. Reduced bladder-outlet resistance may be addressed through bladder-neck reconstruction in a suitably compliant reservoir; achieving dryness must not create unsafe pressure.

Prune-belly syndrome is a triad of deficient abdominal musculature, urinary-tract dilatation/dysfunction and bilateral cryptorchidism. Severity ranges from pulmonary-hypoplasia/renal-failure neonates to relatively preserved function. Assess drainage and renal function, treat infections and respiratory/nutritional needs, use catheterization when necessary, and select reconstruction/orchidopexy/abdominoplasty according to function. Dilatation alone does not justify extensive urinary surgery. Lifelong review is needed for kidney health, emptying, continence and fertility.

### Age, bladder quality and continence strategy
An early neonate with a viable bladder plate is assessed for primary closure with appropriate pelvic management. In older untreated children the plate may be fibrotic or altered and the pelvis less malleable, so osteotomy, reconstruction sequence and continence potential require individualized evaluation. In later childhood assess native capacity/compliance, renal status, outlet anatomy and previous failures before repeating closure or tightening the outlet. A small unsafe bladder may need augmentation with reliable catheter access; severely unsuitable anatomy can require diversion.

Variants can include covered exstrophy, duplicate bladder forms and superior vesical fissure; cloacal exstrophy has additional bowel/spinal complexity and must not be treated as an isolated bladder plate. Associated abnormalities and pubic/pelvic relationships determine genital reconstruction as well as closure. For epispadias, explain plate mobilisation and corporal correction without suggesting complete disassembly is risk free.

In prune belly, evaluate renal dysplasia and urinary drainage separately from impressive dilatation. A large compliant system may not need extensive reconstructive surgery if function/drainage are satisfactory. Bilateral orchidopexy, bladder-emptying support and selected abdominal-wall reconstruction address distinct problems; these procedures can be staged. Pulmonary hypoplasia and neonatal renal failure dominate the severe spectrum. Follow fertility, renal function, infections and continence even when the abdominal appearance improves.

### Bladder-outlet operations and diversion names
Young-Dees-Leadbetter-type bladder-neck reconstruction aims to create a more resistant outlet in appropriate exstrophy anatomy. Selected slings/bulking or other continence procedures have different indications, efficacy and obstruction risks; none should be applied before confirming safe storage. Diversion options include an ileal conduit or a continent catheterizable reservoir/channel, with different stoma, infection and metabolic burdens. Historical ureterosigmoidostomy combines urinary drainage with colon and has major infection/metabolic/malignancy concerns; it is not a default modern reconstruction.

### Bladder augmentation and continent urinary reconstruction

Indications include refractory low capacity/poor compliance that threatens upper tracts or prevents acceptable continence despite catheterization, drugs and selected botulinum treatment; causes include neurogenic bladder and selected exstrophy/outlet reconstructions. Preoperative assessment documents urodynamics, renal function, bowel availability, nutritional status, infection, ability to catheterize and lifelong follow-up. Informed discussion must include dependence on CIC and risk of emergency perforation.

Detubularised ileum is commonly used because of availability and a compliant reservoir. Colon can provide a large patch but produces mucus and electrolyte exchange. Stomach has less mucus and may be considered in selected metabolic situations, but risks haematuria-dysuria syndrome, acid secretion, hypochloraemic alkalosis and ulceration; it is not the routine preferred segment. Ileum/colon can cause hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, particularly when renal function is poor. Ureterocystoplasty avoids intestinal metabolic consequences but requires a suitable dilated ureter and may provide limited capacity. Autoaugmentation has variable durability and smaller capacity gains.

Open the bladder widely, detubularise the bowel to prevent high-pressure peristaltic contractions, create a broad patch and obtain a watertight anastomosis with drainage. Preserve bowel and urinary blood supply. An appendicovesicostomy (Mitrofanoff) or reconfigured ileal Monti channel can allow catheterization through a continent abdominal stoma; it is a channel, not the reservoir itself. Select patients who can follow catheterization/irrigation reliably or have dependable assistance. Bladder-neck surgery must not create obstruction in an unsafe reservoir.

Early complications are leakage, ileus, bleeding, infection and bowel obstruction. Late complications include stones, mucus retention, symptomatic infection, metabolic acidosis, B12 deficiency after relevant ileal use, bowel symptoms, channel stenosis/leakage and spontaneous bladder perforation. Malignancy risk is a long-term consideration; investigation is symptom/risk guided rather than an assumed universal annual cystoscopy regimen. Acute abdominal pain in an augmented patient demands evaluation for perforation even with an initially nondiagnostic scan. Follow reservoir pressures, residuals, renal function, electrolytes, ultrasound and catheterization adherence through transition to adult services.

### Alternatives and postoperative safeguards
The common bowel-based choices are ileocystoplasty, colocystoplasty and selected gastrocystoplasty; less common approaches include ureterocystoplasty and autoaugmentation. Detubularisation reduces coordinated bowel contractions and increases reservoir compliance. Gastrocystoplasty can be less favourable because of painful acid secretion/haematuria-dysuria and alkalosis; do not describe its lower mucus production as absence of serious long-term risk. After augmentation ensure adequate catheter drainage, mucus irrigation when prescribed, and an emergency plan for pain/distension or inability to catheterize.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology (2026)](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology)

questions.title: Duplex systems, ectopic ureter, ureterocele and megaureter
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Duplex systems, ectopic ureter, ureterocele and megaureter

Complete duplication results from two ureteric buds; incomplete duplication from early division of one bud. By the Weigert-Meyer rule, the upper-moiety ureter generally opens inferomedially and is prone to ectopia/ureterocele or obstruction; the lower-moiety ureter opens superolaterally and is prone to reflux. Exceptions exist. A girl who dribbles continuously despite normal voluntary voiding suggests an ectopic ureter opening below the external sphincter; ordinary enuresis is intermittent. Boys' ectopic ureters usually open above the sphincter and cause infection/obstruction rather than continuous leakage.

Assess ultrasound, urine culture, renal function and moiety function. MR urography maps complex anatomy/ectopic insertion; VCUG evaluates reflux and urethra; DMSA or dynamic imaging measures function, while cystoscopy/vaginoscopy can identify outlets. A poorly functioning upper moiety can be treated by upper-pole heminephrectomy with careful preservation of lower-pole blood supply, or by ureteroureterostomy in suitable anatomy. A functioning moiety favours drainage-preserving reconstruction such as ureteroureterostomy or reimplantation. In the stated example with 3% upper and 36% lower function, do not sacrifice the functioning lower moiety; discuss upper-pole surgery versus drainage reconstruction based on anatomy, infections and tissue quality.

A ureterocele is cystic dilatation of the intravesical distal ureter; developmental theories include persistence of Chwalla's membrane and abnormal ureteral incorporation. Classify intravesical versus ectopic, single versus duplex. Cecoureterocele extends into/beyond the bladder neck. Infection, obstruction or retention may require endoscopic incision/puncture for decompression, followed by assessment for induced/persistent reflux and definitive reconstruction. Preserve functioning moieties and consider the bladder-neck effect.

Megaureter is a dilated ureter, commonly described as over 7 mm; categories are obstructed, refluxing, both, or nonobstructed/nonrefluxing, and primary versus secondary. Assess distal obstruction, VUR, bladder dysfunction and renal function with ultrasound, VCUG when indicated and renography. Many primary nonrefluxing cases improve with observation; recurrent febrile infections, symptoms, worsening dilatation or declining function favour intervention. Definitive reimplantation may require tapering, preserving adventitial blood supply. Temporizing drainage is useful in selected infants.

![Original teaching schematic: duplex law. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/duplex-law.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology (2026)](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology)

questions.title: Hypospadias, curvature and graft urethroplasty
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Hypospadias, curvature and graft urethroplasty

Hypospadias combines a ventral ectopic meatus with variable curvature and deficient ventral foreskin; severity depends on curvature, plate/glans quality and penile dimensions as well as meatal site. Classify distal (glanular/coronal/distal shaft), midshaft and proximal (penoscrotal/scrotal/perineal). Disturbed androgen production/action and urethral-fold fusion contribute, with genetic/environmental factors. Preserve the prepuce until a reconstructive plan is made.

Proximal hypospadias with undescended testis, particularly bilateral nonpalpable testes, warrants DSD assessment: electrolytes, endocrine testing, karyotype/genetic evaluation and pelvic/gonadal anatomy under a multidisciplinary team. Routine renal imaging is not required in uncomplicated isolated distal hypospadias. Usual repair timing is infancy, commonly 6-18 months, individualized for health and resources. Goals are straight erection, a functional meatus, durable urethra and acceptable appearance.

At operation deglove and assess curvature with an erection test. Skin tethering may resolve after degloving; persistent curvature requires correction. Mild curvature can be corrected by dorsal plication with awareness of shortening; severe ventral curvature may need plate division and ventral corporotomy/lengthening, often with staged reconstruction. A good distal plate can undergo TIP/Snodgrass: incise the plate longitudinally, tubularise over a catheter and cover with a vascularised intermediate layer before glans closure. Onlay preputial island flap (Duckett onlay) augments a preserved plate; a tubularized island flap is a different operation. Severe proximal/poor-plate and redo cases may benefit from staged graft repair.

Buccal mucosa is useful in redo or deficient local tissue: defat the graft, secure on a vascular bed, allow maturation and then tubularise in a second stage when appropriate. It is a free graft and depends on plasmatic imbibition/revascularisation; an interposition dartos/tunica-vaginalis flap supplies vascular coverage and separates suture lines. Avoid taking scarred or diseased tissue. Preoperative androgen treatment is selective and evidence on benefit/complications is mixed; it is not compulsory.

Complications include fistula, meatal stenosis, urethral stricture, diverticulum, dehiscence, recurrent curvature and cosmetic/functional concerns. Assess stream and obstruction before repairing a fistula. Follow through puberty because late curvature and sexual-function issues may emerge. Balanitis xerotica obliterans/lichen sclerosus may affect foreskin, meatus and urethra; diagnosis is clinical with histology where indicated, treatment ranges from circumcision/topical therapy to specialist urethral reconstruction.

### Named distal repairs and onlay-flap steps
Selected glanular/coronal anatomy without meaningful curvature may suit MAGPI (meatal advancement and glanuloplasty); Mathieu uses a perimeatal flap, and a broad healthy plate can suit Thiersch-Duplay tubularisation. TIP expands options by incising the plate, while GAP (glans approximation) is selected for suitable deep-grooved glanular anatomy. Severe curvature or a poor plate changes the plan. For a Duckett onlay, harvest inner preputial tissue on its vascular pedicle, transfer without twisting, suture its margins as an onlay to the retained urethral plate and cover the reconstruction before glans/skin closure. Distinguish this from a tubularized flap and avoid using a damaged plate merely to preserve a one-stage plan.

![Original teaching schematic: hypospadias plan. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/hypospadias-plan.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [EAU: Hypospadias](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology/chapter/hypospadias)

questions.title: Bladder innervation, urodynamics and neurogenic bladder
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Bladder innervation, urodynamics and neurogenic bladder

Parasympathetic pelvic nerves (S2-S4) mediate detrusor contraction primarily via muscarinic receptors. Sympathetic hypogastric nerves (thoracolumbar) support storage through beta-mediated detrusor relaxation and alpha-mediated outlet contraction. Pudendal somatic fibres (S2-S4) supply the external urethral sphincter. Pontine and cortical control coordinate detrusor contraction with sphincter relaxation.

In spinal dysraphism, combinations of overactive/underactive detrusor and sphincter denervation or dyssynergia occur. Neurological lesion level alone cannot reliably predict bladder behaviour. A hostile bladder has unsafe storage/voiding pressure, poor compliance, detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia and/or incomplete emptying that threatens renal function; a detrusor leak-point pressure near/above 40 cmH2O is a historical risk signal, not the sole treatment threshold.

Urodynamics measures vesical and abdominal pressure; detrusor pressure is their difference. Assess cystometric capacity, compliance (change in volume/change in detrusor pressure), detrusor overactivity, leakage, pressure-flow pattern and residual volume. Video-urodynamics adds reflux/outlet information; EMG helps assess sphincter coordination. Interpret against age, symptoms, infection, bowel status and technical quality. High filling pressure plus low compliance implies unsafe storage; low pressure with high residual suggests inadequate emptying. Demonstrate detrusor-pressure and sphincter patterns schematically.

After MMC repair obtain baseline renal/bladder ultrasound, renal function assessment and an early urological plan; urodynamic timing is individualized but should identify risk before renal injury. Reassess with growth, continence changes, infection or upper-tract deterioration. Clean intermittent catheterization ensures emptying; oxybutynin or another age-appropriate antimuscarinic treats overactivity/poor compliance. Beta-3 agonists and intradetrusor botulinum toxin are selected options when standard treatment is inadequate; dosing and approval differ by age. Alpha blockers target outlet resistance in selected cases. Botox blocks acetylcholine release; its bladder benefit is temporary and CIC may be required. Antibiotics treat symptomatic infection; avoid treating every asymptomatic catheter culture.

Manage constipation, maintain a catheterization plan and monitor kidneys, BP and growth. Refractory unsafe storage may require augmentation and a catheterizable channel. Priorities are renal preservation, safe low-pressure storage, reliable emptying, social continence and independence; a dry child can still have a dangerous bladder.

### Drug and pressure interpretation for a five-mark subpart
Antimuscarinics reduce involuntary contraction and can improve compliance, but cause dry mouth, constipation and sometimes impaired emptying. Beta-3 agonists promote storage-phase relaxation; confirm paediatric indication and BP effects. Botulinum toxin inhibits presynaptic acetylcholine release and can be injected into detrusor for refractory neurogenic overactivity or into an anal sphincter for selected outlet achalasia. Its effect is temporary; reassess pressures and emptying rather than assume continence means safe storage. CIC is a drainage method, not a drug, and is often required alongside pharmacotherapy.

![Original teaching schematic: neurobladder. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/neurobladder.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology (2026)](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology)

questions.title: VUR, UTIs and ureteric reimplantation
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### VUR, UTIs and ureteric reimplantation

Primary VUR is failure of the ureterovesical antireflux mechanism, often due to a short intramural tunnel. Secondary VUR results from raised bladder pressure or outlet dysfunction. Grade I reflux reaches ureter only; II reaches collecting system without dilatation; III has mild/moderate dilatation; IV has moderate dilatation/tortuosity with blunted fornices; V has gross dilatation/tortuosity and loss of papillary impressions. Reflux nephropathy includes congenital dysplasia and acquired scarring after febrile pyelonephritis; reflux does not by itself explain every scar.

Risk factors for childhood UTI include VUR/obstruction, bladder-bowel dysfunction, incomplete emptying, instrumentation and selected congenital anomalies. Obtain a reliable urine specimen and culture before treatment where practical. Ultrasound identifies anatomy; VCUG defines reflux and urethra; DMSA assesses cortical defects/scarring. A top-down strategy starts with renal parenchymal assessment in selected febrile UTI cases and uses VCUG selectively, rather than studying reflux first in everyone. Imaging strategies vary with age and guideline; radiation and whether results change management matter.

Treat infection promptly and manage constipation/voiding dysfunction. Observation with or without prophylaxis is selected according to grade, age, renal abnormalities and febrile-UTI risk. Surgery is considered for breakthrough febrile UTI despite appropriate treatment, persistent high-risk reflux/renal deterioration, poor feasibility of surveillance/prophylaxis, or associated anatomical indications. Correct unsafe bladder pressures first.

Endoscopic injection creates a supportive mound beneath the intramural ureter. STING places the needle subureterically; HIT uses hydrodistention and injection within the ureteral tunnel, with double-HIT variants. Advantages are short intervention and low morbidity; success is lower in higher grades/complex anatomy and reinjection or reimplantation may be needed. Risks include obstruction, persistence and recurrent reflux.

Open reimplantation options include intravesical Cohen cross-trigonal, Politano-Leadbetter and Glenn-Anderson advancement, and extravesical Lich-Gregoir. A tunnel-length/ureter-diameter ratio around 5:1 (Paquin principle) is a useful surgical concept, while blood supply and tension-free alignment remain crucial. Vesicoscopic Cohen uses intravesical ports/pneumovesicum; robotic reimplantation commonly uses an extravesical approach. Mobilise without devascularizing, preserve nerves, construct the tunnel and confirm unobstructed drainage. Bilateral extravesical dissection risks transient retention. Complications include obstruction, persistent reflux, urine leak and voiding dysfunction.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology (2026)](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology)

questions.title: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: embryology, prognostication and stabilization
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: embryology, prognostication and stabilization

### Development and types
The diaphragm develops from the septum transversum (central tendon), paired pleuroperitoneal folds, dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus (crura), and muscular ingrowth from the body wall. Its descent explains the phrenic nerve supply from C3-C5. A simple failure-of-closure account is incomplete: abnormal pleuroperitoneal-fold mesenchyme and disturbed muscle development contribute to the defect; pulmonary hypoplasia may precede and then be aggravated by herniation (dual-hit model).

Bochdalek defects are posterolateral, usually left sided; Morgagni defects are anterior/retrosternal; central tendon defects are uncommon. Eventration is an intact but deficiently muscular diaphragm, rather than a true hole. Distinguish a hiatal hernia through the oesophageal hiatus from CDH. Label the heart, liver, bowel, lung and defect in a schematic.

### Antenatal assessment
Ultrasound shows intrathoracic stomach/bowel, mediastinal shift and a small ipsilateral lung. Assess side, liver position, observed-to-expected lung-to-head ratio (o/e LHR), defect severity, associated cardiac/genetic abnormalities and polyhydramnios. Fetal MRI estimates total fetal lung volume and liver herniation. Large defects, liver up, low o/e LHR or lung volume, and major associated anomalies worsen prognosis. Postnatally, pulmonary hypertension, ventricular dysfunction, oxygen requirement, oxygenation index and ECMO requirement add physiological information. Survival figures must specify whether they describe all diagnosed pregnancies, live births or treated infants.

### Immediate and intensive care management
Plan delivery in a centre with neonatal intensive care and paediatric surgery. Intubate a symptomatic known-CDH neonate and decompress the stomach with an orogastric tube; bag-mask ventilation can inflate intrathoracic bowel. Maintain warmth, analgesia and careful handling. Use gentle pressure-limited ventilation; avoid volutrauma and accept appropriate permissive hypercapnia while following pH, lactate and perfusion. Conventional ventilation is commonly first line; high-frequency ventilation is a rescue option when acceptable gas exchange cannot be obtained within safe pressures. Titrate oxygen to preductal saturation and assess pre/postductal difference. Echocardiography defines pulmonary hypertension and biventricular function; pulmonary vasodilators and vasoactive drugs should follow that physiology, rather than be given automatically.

Give cautious isotonic fluid aliquots with reassessment; excessive fluid worsens pulmonary oedema. Monitor arterial gases, BP, lactate trend, urine output, electrolytes and echocardiography. Refractory cardiopulmonary failure may require ECMO in an eligible infant. Repair follows physiological stabilization, rather than an arbitrary time after birth: acceptable oxygenation/ventilation on stable settings, satisfactory BP and urine output, improving lactate and controlled pulmonary hypertension. Reduce viscera and obtain tension-free closure; use a patch for a large defect. Severe physiology and large defects favour open repair; selected stable infants may undergo minimally invasive repair.

### Sudden acidosis and long-term issues
Check displaced/blocked tube, pneumothorax, worsening pulmonary hypertension, ventricular failure, sepsis, inadequate perfusion and bowel compromise. Check the circuit and tube, examine, obtain bedside imaging/echo and correct the cause promptly. Follow recurrence, pulmonary disease, reflux, growth, hearing and neurodevelopment. The historical shift is from urgent anatomical repair to lung-protective stabilization and delayed repair. FETO is a specialised option for selected severe fetal CDH, with prematurity and balloon-removal risks; it is not routine treatment for every fetus.

### Lung pathology and the management implication
Affected lungs have fewer/smaller airways and alveolar units and a reduced pulmonary vascular bed. Abnormal vascular muscularisation/reactivity contributes to high pulmonary vascular resistance, with right-heart pressure load and possible left-ventricular dysfunction. Consequently, high-pressure ventilation cannot simply 'inflate the missing lung'; overdistension of relatively preserved lung worsens injury and haemodynamics. Gentle ventilation, echocardiography-directed circulation support and delayed repair address this physiological disease alongside the anatomical defect.

### Fetal circulation, screening, fetal surgery and EXIT

Oxygenated placental blood returns by umbilical vein; much passes through the ductus venosus to IVC. Preferential streaming across foramen ovale enters left atrium/ventricle and supplies brain/coronaries; right-ventricular output mostly passes from pulmonary artery through ductus arteriosus to descending aorta. Two umbilical arteries return blood to placenta. At birth cord clamping increases systemic resistance; lung aeration lowers pulmonary resistance, increasing pulmonary return and functionally closing the foramen ovale. Rising oxygen and reduced prostaglandin activity promote ductal closure; fetal channels subsequently remodel. Draw flow arrows and distinguish mixing from separate adult circulations.

First-trimester screening combines ultrasound/nuchal translucency with biochemical tests or cell-free DNA according to programme; cfDNA is a screening test, not definitive diagnosis. Second-trimester anatomy ultrasound assesses brain/spine, face, heart, thorax, abdomen, kidneys, limbs, placenta and fluid. Maternal AFP can identify open NTD risk. CVS/amniocentesis provide diagnostic genetic sampling with procedure risks. Fetal MRI adds CNS, thoracic and complex pelvic anatomy but complements ultrasound; it is not universal screening. Down-syndrome ultrasound findings can include increased nuchal thickness, cardiac defects, echogenic bowel and short long bones, but absence does not exclude trisomy 21.

Fetal intervention is reserved for selected conditions where prenatal treatment plausibly improves outcome: severe CDH (FETO), selected LUTO shunting/cystoscopy, MMC repair, selected obstructing CPAM drainage and highly selected fetal tumours/other lesions. Maternal risks include anaesthetic/operative complications, haemorrhage, infection, membrane rupture, preterm labour and uterine-scar effects on future pregnancies. Selection requires detailed anatomy/genetics, realistic prognosis and maternal informed consent; fetal benefit does not erase maternal risk.

EXIT (ex utero intrapartum treatment) maintains uteroplacental gas exchange during partial fetal delivery while securing an airway or completing a selected life-saving step. Indications include predicted severe airway obstruction from neck/oral masses and selected thoracic/airway conditions. Plan maternal anaesthesia/uterine relaxation, placental position, fetal monitoring, airway sequence (laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, tracheostomy) and haemorrhage control with multidisciplinary rehearsal. Once a reliable airway/support is established, clamp the cord and complete delivery; prolonged placental support has limits.

### Named screening tests
First-trimester combined screening uses nuchal translucency with PAPP-A and free beta-hCG. The second-trimester quadruple test combines AFP, hCG, unconjugated estriol and inhibin A; a triple test omits inhibin A. Cell-free DNA has strong screening performance for selected aneuploidies but does not diagnose all structural/genetic disorders. Increased AFP can prompt open-NTD evaluation with targeted ultrasound; a screen result requires interpretation and appropriate confirmatory counselling/testing.

![Original teaching schematic: cdh development. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/cdh-development.svg)

![Original teaching schematic: fetal circulation. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/fetal-circulation.svg)

questions.title: Renal scintigraphy, diuretic renography and L,L-EC
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Renal scintigraphy, diuretic renography and L,L-EC

99mTc-MAG3 is extracted predominantly by proximal tubular secretion and provides good images at lower renal function; 99mTc-L,L-ethylenedicysteine (EC) is another tubular agent. 99mTc-DTPA is filtered at the glomerulus and can estimate GFR but has lower extraction. 99mTc-DMSA is retained in renal cortex and is used for cortical anatomy/scarring and relative cortical function; it is not the usual drainage agent. The paper's 'LLEC scan' is interpreted as L,L-EC renal scintigraphy, rather than an unrelated test.

For a diuretic study, ensure hydration, review prior anatomy, select an age/weight-adjusted tracer activity and avoid a distended bladder; catheterization is selected for reflux, neurogenic bladder or drainage concerns. Dynamic images document perfusion, uptake and excretion. Furosemide increases urine flow, with F-0 or F+20-type protocols selected by the service. Quantify differential function, time-activity curves, drainage after diuretic, cortical transit and postvoid/gravity-assisted drainage.

Prompt washout argues against significant obstruction. Delayed washout can arise from obstruction, a very large compliant reservoir, dehydration, poor renal function or a full bladder. Traditional half-time categories (under 10 minutes reassuring, over 20 minutes potentially obstructed) must be interpreted with the whole study; half-time alone is not a diagnosis. Compare serial studies using similar technique. Draw a normal descending curve and an obstructed rising/plateau curve after diuretic, labelled as illustrative.

Captopril renography investigates suspected renovascular hypertension by reducing angiotensin-II-mediated efferent arteriolar support of filtration; a stenotic kidney may show reduced uptake/function and delayed transit after ACE inhibition. It has limited sensitivity in bilateral disease, small children and impaired renal function, and requires BP/safety monitoring. Other indications for isotope imaging include differential function before reconstructive surgery, ectopic/duplex anatomy, cortical scars and transplant perfusion/function.

### Surgical energy, laser, ultrasonic devices and CUSA

Monopolar electrosurgery sends current from the active electrode through the patient to a return electrode; it allows cutting/coagulation but risks return-pad burns, coupling and remote thermal injury. Bipolar current passes between two tips, confining the circuit; advanced bipolar devices combine pressure with controlled energy to seal appropriate vessels. Observe each device's vessel-size limit and cooling needs; a seal is not assured merely because tissue was grasped.

Ultrasonic instruments convert high-frequency mechanical vibration into tissue cutting/coaptation with heat; there is no electrical current through the patient, but the blade can remain very hot. They can injure adjacent bowel/ureter/nerve by residual heat. CUSA means Cavitron Ultrasonic Surgical Aspirator: ultrasonic vibration fragments softer tissue with simultaneous irrigation/aspiration, facilitating dissection around firmer vascular/ductal structures, particularly in liver surgery; it does not eliminate bleeding risk. Argon/plasma devices and other ablative instruments have site-specific uses and gas/thermal hazards.

LASER is light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. Wavelength, absorption, pulse duration and energy density govern penetration and thermal effect. CO2 is strongly absorbed by water and used for superficial precise cutting; Nd:YAG penetrates more deeply; pulsed-dye targets superficial vascular chromophores; holmium is important for endourological stone fragmentation. Applications include airway lesions, selected vascular/skin lesions and endoscopy. Use wavelength-appropriate eye protection, smoke extraction and airway-fire precautions; protect adjacent tissue and avoid claiming all lasers are equally safe for every lesion.

Energy complications include burns, delayed perforation, bleeding from an inadequate seal, smoke exposure, fire and device interaction. Inspect insulation/return electrodes, use the lowest effective energy, maintain visual control and keep heated tips away from vulnerable tissue. A good comparison states mechanism, intended use, advantages and particular limitations, rather than labelling one technology superior in all operations.

![Original teaching schematic: renogram. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/renogram.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [SNMMI/EANM paediatric diuresis renography guideline](https://snmmi.org/Web/Clinical-Practice/Procedure-Standards/Standards/Diuresis-Renography-in-Infants-and-Children.aspx)

questions.title: CSF circulation, hydrocephalus and shunt complications
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### CSF circulation, hydrocephalus and shunt complications

CSF is produced mainly by choroid plexus: lateral ventricles -> foramina of Monro -> third ventricle -> aqueduct -> fourth ventricle -> foramina of Magendie/Luschka -> cisterns/subarachnoid space -> venous and lymphatic clearance pathways. Hydrocephalus is disturbed CSF dynamics with ventricular enlargement; obstructive disease blocks an intraventricular pathway, whereas communicating disease often impairs downstream circulation/absorption. Causes include aqueduct stenosis, posterior-fossa lesions, haemorrhage, infection and congenital malformations.

Assess head growth/fontanelle in infants, vomiting/headache, papilloedema, developmental change and focal signs. Ultrasound through an open fontanelle, MRI and selected urgent CT demonstrate anatomy; ventricular size alone does not define clinical severity. VP shunting diverts CSF to the peritoneum. ETV creates an opening in the third-ventricle floor into the basal cisterns and is most suitable for selected obstructive disease; age, aetiology and prior shunt affect success. Choroid-plexus cauterisation is an additional selected strategy in some infant settings.

Early shunt problems include infection, blockage, malposition, haemorrhage and CSF leak; late problems include disconnection, migration, overdrainage, subdural collections, abdominal pseudocyst and bowel perforation. Suspected infection needs cultures and neurosurgical source-control/antimicrobial planning. Suspected malfunction is a clinical emergency; a small ventricle does not exclude failure. Slit-ventricle syndrome involves symptomatic shunted patients with small ventricles and abnormal pressure dynamics, potentially from overdrainage or intermittent obstruction. Management may require valve adjustment/antisiphon strategies or selected revision, guided by physiology.

Aqueductal stenosis may be treated by ETV or a shunt according to suitability. Prevent shunt complications through sterile technique, appropriate perioperative prophylaxis, sound catheter placement and structured surveillance. Families need clear warning symptoms and access to assessment. Agenesis of the corpus callosum is a developmental malformation with variable associated anomalies and developmental outcomes; investigate genetics/other CNS abnormalities and provide supportive neurodevelopmental care rather than treating it as an obstructive lesion automatically.

### Neural-tube defects, tethered cord and the MOMS trial

Neural-tube defects include open myelomeningocele/myeloschisis and closed dysraphism such as lipomyelomeningocele, dermal sinus and split-cord malformation. Folate status, maternal diabetes, medications and genetic factors contribute. Prevention includes preconception folic acid and risk-specific higher-dose strategies through obstetric guidance. Ultrasound and maternal serum AFP support antenatal detection; detailed neurosonography/MRI assess associated CNS findings.

For open MMC, protect the lesion with sterile moist nonadherent material, position to avoid pressure, maintain warmth, assess neurological level, urinary function and hydrocephalus, and organise early neurosurgical closure after stabilization. Prevent infection and latex exposure. Follow hydrocephalus/Chiari II, lower-limb function, orthopaedic problems, renal/bladder function, bowel continence, skin pressure injuries and learning/psychosocial needs.

Tethered cord is pathological traction on the spinal cord, caused by lipoma, thick/tight filum, split-cord malformation, dermal sinus or postoperative scarring. Cutaneous signs, pain, progressive weakness, deformity or new bladder deterioration prompt MRI and neurological/urological assessment. Detethering is indicated for suitable progressive/symptomatic disease; prophylactic surgery in asymptomatic variants is individualized and controversial. Diastematomyelia/split cord has two hemicords separated by a bony/fibrous septum with one or two dural sacs; define the full anatomy before treatment.

Chiari I is predominantly tonsillar descent, Chiari II associates with MMC and hindbrain displacement, III involves hindbrain herniation into an encephalocele, and IV is a historical term for cerebellar hypoplasia. In symptomatic Chiari II first assess hydrocephalus/shunt function; selected persistent brainstem compression needs neurosurgical decompression.

The MOMS randomized trial compared prenatal and postnatal MMC repair in selected pregnancies. Prenatal repair reduced need for CSF shunting and improved some motor outcomes, with maternal uterine-scar and prematurity risks. It did not eliminate neurological/urological disability. Candidates require stringent maternal/fetal assessment and specialist facilities; discuss lifelong maternal obstetric consequences and possible repeat fetal/postnatal interventions. Outcomes from selected trial patients cannot be extrapolated to every fetus.

- [MOMS randomized trial: prenatal versus postnatal MMC repair](https://www.nejm.org/doi/abs/10.1056/nejmoa1014379)

questions.title: Duplex systems, ectopic ureter, ureterocele and megaureter
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Duplex systems, ectopic ureter, ureterocele and megaureter

Complete duplication results from two ureteric buds; incomplete duplication from early division of one bud. By the Weigert-Meyer rule, the upper-moiety ureter generally opens inferomedially and is prone to ectopia/ureterocele or obstruction; the lower-moiety ureter opens superolaterally and is prone to reflux. Exceptions exist. A girl who dribbles continuously despite normal voluntary voiding suggests an ectopic ureter opening below the external sphincter; ordinary enuresis is intermittent. Boys' ectopic ureters usually open above the sphincter and cause infection/obstruction rather than continuous leakage.

Assess ultrasound, urine culture, renal function and moiety function. MR urography maps complex anatomy/ectopic insertion; VCUG evaluates reflux and urethra; DMSA or dynamic imaging measures function, while cystoscopy/vaginoscopy can identify outlets. A poorly functioning upper moiety can be treated by upper-pole heminephrectomy with careful preservation of lower-pole blood supply, or by ureteroureterostomy in suitable anatomy. A functioning moiety favours drainage-preserving reconstruction such as ureteroureterostomy or reimplantation. In the stated example with 3% upper and 36% lower function, do not sacrifice the functioning lower moiety; discuss upper-pole surgery versus drainage reconstruction based on anatomy, infections and tissue quality.

A ureterocele is cystic dilatation of the intravesical distal ureter; developmental theories include persistence of Chwalla's membrane and abnormal ureteral incorporation. Classify intravesical versus ectopic, single versus duplex. Cecoureterocele extends into/beyond the bladder neck. Infection, obstruction or retention may require endoscopic incision/puncture for decompression, followed by assessment for induced/persistent reflux and definitive reconstruction. Preserve functioning moieties and consider the bladder-neck effect.

Megaureter is a dilated ureter, commonly described as over 7 mm; categories are obstructed, refluxing, both, or nonobstructed/nonrefluxing, and primary versus secondary. Assess distal obstruction, VUR, bladder dysfunction and renal function with ultrasound, VCUG when indicated and renography. Many primary nonrefluxing cases improve with observation; recurrent febrile infections, symptoms, worsening dilatation or declining function favour intervention. Definitive reimplantation may require tapering, preserving adventitial blood supply. Temporizing drainage is useful in selected infants.

![Original teaching schematic: duplex law. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/duplex-law.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology (2026)](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology)

questions.title: Vascular tumours, malformations and Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Vascular tumours, malformations and Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon

Distinguish proliferative vascular tumours from structural vascular malformations. Infantile haemangiomas appear/grow after birth and then involute; congenital haemangiomas are fully formed at birth and have different involution patterns. Venous/lymphatic/capillary malformations are typically low flow; arteriovenous malformations have high-flow shunts. Name the classification version when asked: older simple/combined categories occur in past papers, while the current ISSVA structure emphasizes flow and biological grouping. Do not describe all vascular anomalies as 'haemangiomas'.

Assess depth, extent, flow, functional compromise and syndromic distribution with examination and Doppler; MRI maps deep lesions. Infantile haemangioma treatment is indicated for threatening airway/vision, ulceration, disfigurement risk or significant systemic effects. Propranolol acts through early vasoconstriction and longer effects on angiogenic signalling; assess cardiac/respiratory contraindications and educate about bradycardia, bronchospasm and hypoglycaemia, especially with fasting. Topical timolol suits selected small superficial lesions; corticosteroids/other systemic agents are selected alternatives. Laser and surgery have defined roles; they are not always first treatment for the proliferative phase.

Venous malformations may be managed with compression, image-guided sclerotherapy, selected excision and treatment of pain/thrombosis; extensive disease may need targeted systemic agents under a vascular-anomaly service. Lymphatic malformations respond to lesion-specific sclerotherapy/resection, with selected sirolimus or pathway-directed treatment for complex disease. CLOVES (congenital lipomatous overgrowth, vascular malformations, epidermal naevi, spinal/skeletal abnormalities) is within the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum.

Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon is severe thrombocytopenia/consumptive coagulopathy associated chiefly with kaposiform haemangioendothelioma or tufted angioma, not ordinary infantile haemangioma. Assess platelets, fibrinogen, coagulation and haemodynamic risk; management is urgent multidisciplinary tumour-directed therapy (commonly sirolimus-based/selected vincristine strategies), with blood products for bleeding/procedural need rather than automatic repeated platelet replacement. The historical term hepatic infantile haemangioendothelioma often refers to infantile hepatic haemangioma; distinguish focal congenital, multifocal and diffuse patterns, and assess high-output failure and consumptive hypothyroidism. Treat symptomatic disease and associated endocrine/cardiac consequences, with selected embolisation/surgery for refractory or anatomically appropriate lesions.

### Updated labels and drug mechanisms
The 2025 ISSVA classification also introduces potentially unique vascular anomaly (PUVA) terminology; use the full current schema for unusual lesions. Propranolol/timolol are beta blockers; systemic corticosteroids have anti-inflammatory/antiangiogenic effects and are alternatives in selected infantile-haemangioma cases. Historical interferon/vincristine treatments have toxicity limitations and are not routine first-line substitutes for propranolol. Sirolimus acts through mTOR and pathway-directed agents target selected molecular abnormalities in complex malformations; do not imply that every infantile haemangioma needs them.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [ISSVA Classification and Glossary (2025)](https://www.issva.org/classification)
